articles.title: 'Lips must move': Bengal CM Suvendu Adhikari warns schools of aid cut over Vande Mataram rendition
articles.summary: KOLKATA: West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari on Thursday warned schools that financial aid and other government support would be stopped if th.
articles.body: KOLKATA: West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari on Thursday warned schools that financial aid and other government support would be stopped if the mandatory singing of the full version of Vande Mataram during school prayers was not strictly followed.Addressing the annual programme of Vivekananda Vidya Bharati Vikas Parishad, an RSS-affiliated organisation, at Ramakrishna Mission in Kolkata's Golpark, Adhikari alleged that the state's education system had been "brought to the brink of destruction" under successive governments in the past.He said the current BJP dispensation was carrying out reforms to restore Indian culture, traditions and nationalist values in school education."A few people had objected to singing the complete rendition of Vande Mataram. I told them that government aid would stop. Then they budged, but only partially. They stood up, but did not move lips. Then I told them that lips must move as well," the CM said, sporting a smile.Adhikari claimed that English-language education was curtailed during the Left Front regime, while the TMC era had "distorted school curricula through appeasement politics".He said words such as 'maa', 'jal' and 'akash' in school curricula were deliberately replaced with 'amma', 'pani' and 'asmaan', respectively.He said the "subtle changes" were in contrast to the pedagogic ideas of stalwarts like Iswar Chandra Vidyasagar and Swami Vivekananda.The CM also accused the previous government of committing the "unforgivable crime" of banning the National Cadet Corps (NCC) in educational institutions."I met defence minister Rajnath Singh recently and made two requests: First, I urged him to build more Sainik Schools in the state, and second, I told him I will write to him seeking permission to make NCC mandatory in schools and colleges. I have already sent him that letter and received his assurance to do the needful," the CM said.Adhikari's remarks came amid continuing political disagreements in West Bengal over education policy, curriculum changes, teacher recruitment and the role of ideology in educational institutions."The people of West Bengal provide time when it comes to change and giving opportunities. They gave time to the Congress after Independence, gave sufficient opportunities to the subsequent United Front and Left Front governments, and for the last 15 years they had given time to the TMC," he said."But they also brought about the change in the state at the right time, else an Islamic education system of Bangladesh would have been replicated here," Adhikari said, referring to the state's political history.He claimed that if the education policy followed during the last decade of TMC rule had continued for some more time, "our values, our heritage, tradition, patriotism and nationalism were pushed to the brink of getting lost forever".Adhikari said people had brought about political change in the state at the "right time", arguing that reforms were needed to restore the education system and foster patriotism among young people.Claiming that the school education system during the previous TMC era contributed to "creating divisions among children", the CM said, "Scholarships from classes 5-8 were made available only to Muslim students while the opportunity was denied to students of other communities."He claimed that the syllabus referred to the removal of the Tata group from Singur but did not mention the contribution of Syama Prasad Mookerjee in the formation of West Bengal."The name of former state minister Partha Chatterjee, an accused in school recruitment scam, was included, while the names of freedom fighters such as Khudiram Bose and Matangini Hazra were difficult to find in textbooks," he alleged.Turning to the political debate surrounding the recent unrest at Jadavpur University and slogans relating to Kashmir and Palestine, the chief minister launched a scathing attack on dissident voices within the institution."Bengal is the land of Netaji and Shyamaprasad. Swami Vivekananda was born in Kolkata. And on this land you will say 'Kashmir maange azaadi'! There are no rallies when Pahalgam happens, but during Operation Sindoor, you say, stop the war. Do we have to tolerate these things? You will write 'Free Palestine' on the walls of Jadavpur? Write 'Free PoK'. articles.title: In 1982, Ralph Lauren bought land around a century-old Colorado barn; decades later it had grown into a 17,000-acre ranch and wildlife preserve
articles.summary: US News: In 1982, Ralph Lauren came across an aging wooden barn beneath Colorado’s San Juan Mountains and immediately saw something others might have overlooke.
articles.body: In 1982, Ralph Lauren came across an aging wooden barn beneath Colorado’s San Juan Mountains and immediately saw something others might have overlooked. The nearly century-old Vance barn stood on land outside Ridgway, surrounded by mountain scenery and open meadows. Lauren and his wife, Ricky, fell in love with the property and began building what would eventually become the Double RL Ranch. What started with a historic barn and a relatively modest piece of land grew over the following decades into a sprawling 17,000-acre landscape combining family life, cattle ranching, wildlife habitat and Lauren’s enduring fascination with the American West. In its own account of the property, Ralph Lauren describes the ranch as both a home and an expression of a longstanding Western dream.The century-old barn that started Ralph Lauren’s Colorado dreamThe story of the Double RL Ranch begins with the Vance barn, built in 1905 by Thomas Vance at the base of Colorado’s San Juan Mountains. According to Ralph Lauren’s account, the enormous structure was designed to shelter dairy cattle through severe mountain winters and was constructed from lumber hand-cut from nearby forests. The barn eventually became recognisable to a much wider audience after appearing in Marlboro television commercials. Lauren first encountered it in 1982, when he and Ricky were searching for land in the American West. The couple had considered properties in Utah and Wyoming, but the Colorado landscape surrounding the barn captured their imagination. Lauren later recalled that seeing the mountains and the old structure gave him an immediate sense that the property was special.From neglected property to a carefully preserved ranchWhen Lauren acquired the land, the historic barn was no longer in pristine condition. Ralph Lauren’s feature explains that its floor, porch and hayloft required extensive renovation. The restoration was eventually completed in 2000, while new family and guest buildings were positioned carefully around the landscape. Lauren has described his reluctance to build extensively on the property because he valued the appearance of undisturbed land. Instead, homes were placed in low, inconspicuous locations and partially hidden among trees. The approach reflected a broader philosophy: the buildings were meant to belong to the landscape rather than overwhelm it. Over time, the ranch developed into a distinctive combination of historic architecture, family spaces and open Colorado country, while retaining the character that attracted Lauren to the property in the first place.A 17,000-acre working cattle operationThe Double RL Ranch eventually expanded to roughly 17,000 acres and remained a genuine working cattle operation rather than simply becoming a private retreat. Ralph Lauren’s own published material describes the property as a world-renowned cattle ranch, while another Ralph Lauren feature notes that around 800 Angus and South Devon steers and heifers graze across the ranch. Cowboys move the cattle between pastures on horseback, maintaining a distinctly traditional approach to ranch life. The operation also has a direct connection to Lauren’s businesses: the ranch has supplied beef to Ralph Lauren restaurants in New York and Chicago. This combination of livestock, working cowboys and expansive pastureland gives the property an agricultural purpose alongside its role as the Lauren family’s Colorado home.Where cattle country meets a wildlife preserveThe ranch's significance extends beyond cattle. Ralph Lauren describes the 17,000-acre property as a place where eagles, elk and deer can remain undisturbed among piñon pines and wild sunflowers. That coexistence between ranching and wildlife is central to the character of the Double RL Ranch. Rather than treating the landscape simply as a backdrop for a luxury home, the property has retained large areas of open habitat alongside its agricultural operations. The result is an unusual landscape where cattle grazing, wildlife and the Lauren family’s connection to the American West exist together. The restored Vance barn, meanwhile, remains a physical reminder of the land’s history, linking the ranch today with the working agricultural property Lauren first encountered more than four decades ago.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: This California town with 27 apartments and a local post office is still looking for a buyer. The price has come down to $5.9 million
articles.summary: US News: Campo, an entire town in California, just an hour away from San Diego, has been on sale for years. Now the price has hit its lowest as it did not get .
articles.body: Campo, an entire town in California, just an hour away from San Diego, has been on sale for years. Now the price has hit its lowest as it did not get any luck. The town has its own local post office, a border patrol facility, a church, a VFW (Veterans of Foreign Wars) post, 27 apartments and a hardware store. This isn't the first time Campo has hit the market. The town was listed in 2019 and again in 2024, when it was priced at $6.5 million before being taken off the market. Now it's again on the market with a price of $5,995,000.The current owner, John Ray, has owned the town for 22 years. According to 10News, Ray said he hasn't had the time to develop the property, and so far, it hasn't sold. The listing agent, Nick Hernandez, said the sale covers a specific portion of the area. "It's bringing in about forty thousand a month in current rents," Nick said.The parcels for sale are not considered historical land, according to Nick. But they sit within a town steeped in history as Campo was once home to a military base in World War II."The opportunity extends to revitalizing currently vacant buildings within the town, a move that could add substantial income by introducing new or enhanced services like gyms, laundromats, daycares, or community centers, directly responding to the desires and needs of the local population," reads the real estate listing.History of the townAccording to California Post, the location became prominent in 1885 when the Gaskill brothers constructed the fortress-like Campo Stone Store on-site using four-foot-thick walls to protect against border raids. During World War II, the area changed massively when the US Army absorbed the land to construct Camp Lockett, building a sprawling network of military barracks to garrison the legendary Buffalo Soldiers of the 10th and 28th Cavalry Regiments, the last horse-mounted units in US military history.Following the war, these exact military structures were preserved rather than demolished, transitioning into private ownership in the late 1950s where they were converted into residential apartments and long-term commercial spaces that still stand at the address today, the report said.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.summary: BENGALURU: The Karnataka government on Thursday suspended IAS officer Gyanendra Kumar Gangwar, who is facing allegations linked to irregularities in t.
articles.body: BENGALURU: The Karnataka government on Thursday suspended IAS officer Gyanendra Kumar Gangwar, who is facing allegations linked to irregularities in the KPSC recruitment process.Gangwar is currently in CID custody as the agency probes irregularities at the Karnataka Public Service Commission (KPSC). The Directorate of Enforcement (ED) is separately investigating the case."In exercise of the powers conferred under Rule 3(2) read with 3(3) of the All India Services (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1969, Gyanendra Kumar Gangwar, IAS (KN: 2016), is placed under suspension with immediate effect and until further orders, pending further investigation by the Criminal Investigation Department," the government order said.During his suspension, the officer will be paid subsistence allowance in accordance with Rule 4 of All India Service (Discipline and Appeal) Rules 1969. He will also not be allowed to leave the headquarters under any circumstances without the written permission of the State Government.CID officials arrested Gangwar on August 29 in connection with irregularities in the KPSC recruitment examination for veterinary officers, following two days of intense questioning.Official sources said Gangwar was questioned as he had served as the controller of examinations at the KPSC from February 2024 to March 2026.He was taken into custody for allegedly not cooperating with the investigation, they said.A 2016-batch IAS officer, Gangwar is currently serving as director of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSME) in the Department of Industries and Commerce.The CID is probing allegations of irregularities in the recruitment examination, including the handling of examination records and OMR sheets, as well as the role of involved officials and others.Days before his arrest, Gangwar's whereabouts had triggered controversy after he was reportedly "missing" following ED searches in connection with the alleged KPSC irregularities.However, state home minister Priyank Kharge later said Gangwar had informed him that he had gone to his native place in Uttar Pradesh, citing a family emergency involving his father's health.The ED officials subsequently also conducted searches at Gangwar's premises.In its preamble, the suspension order cited the deputy director, Directorate of Enforcement, Bangalore Zonal Office, as stating that material seized during the search and seizure operation under section 17 of the PMLA, 2002, indicates corruption was prevalent in the recruitment processes conducted by the KPSC, which is solely attributable to the controller of examinations of the KPSC (i.e.) Gyanendra Kumar Gangwar, IAS.It further cited that, "The Director General of Police, Criminal Investigation Department (CID), Bengaluru, has stated that Gangwar was arrested on August 29 in connection with a case registered at the Vidhana Soudha Police Station under section 318(3) of the BNS and Section 10 of the Karnataka Public Examination (Measures for Prevention of Corruption and Unfair Means in Recruitment) Act 2023, which is articles.title: Israel’s siege on Gaza is forcing dentists to operate in the streets
articles.summary: Scarce resources and office space mean that dental work is a luxury for most people in Gaza.
articles.body:
Dr. Rizq Sufyan Abo Halima operates a dental clinic in Gaza City out of a tent due to the destruction of his previous clinics during Israel's war, facing challenges of high costs and limited supply of properties.

The scarcity of materials and high rent prices in Gaza have forced Dr. Abo Halima to use a tent as a cost-effective alternative for his clinic, allowing him to charge patients less for dental procedures.

Patients in Gaza are faced with difficult choices due to the economic hardships caused by the war, with some opting for tooth extraction over costly fillings as a result of the high prices of dental treatments.

Gaza City, Gaza Strip – In the stifling heat of Gaza City, Dr Rizq Sufyan Abo Halima sits in a small tent pitched in an alleyway, waiting for his next patient.

The tent was a last resort for the doctor, given that the high demand and low supply of properties in the Gaza Strip as a result of Israel's genocidal war have made finding an affordable surgery impossible.

"The stifling rise in temperatures was my first challenge," he told Al Jazeera. "I had to adjust the corners of the tent and lift it at the ends to allow air to pass through."

His old clinic, Smile One, in Sheikh Zayed City in northern Gaza, was bombed during the early days of the war in 2023.

The 31-year-old built a new clinic in May last year, next to where his current tent is pitched, in Gaza City's al-Nasr neighbourhood. But three months later, it too was destroyed when Israeli forces assaulted the area, just weeks before the ceasefire last October.

He is now forced to conduct operations and other emergency dental procedures in the tent close to the ruins of his former surgery. When the electricity supply stops, which is frequent, there is little he can do but sit in his tent and wait for the power to come back on.

Finding another office would be the obvious solution, but residential and commercial units are hard to find in Gaza and those few that remain are unaffordable.

More than four in five buildings in Gaza City and northern Gaza have been completely destroyed or severely damaged in Israel's war, according to the United Nations Satellite Centre (UNOSAT).

Fewer than one in five buildings in Gaza can still be used and Israel's ban on building materials has made repairs impossible. That has created a skewed supply situation, which has made prices of office spaces or homes unaffordable.

"Before the war, I used to rent an entire apartment for my clinic for 500 shekels ($166) a month, but today I cannot afford the prices of remaining apartments at all," he said. Now, the cost is closer to $1,000.

Using a tent is the cheapest alternative Dr Abo Halima could find, and he does not want to pass on what he calls the excessive price of building rent to his customers, who are already suffering immense personal and financial hardships.

"If I had rented an apartment for my clinic instead of a tent, the cost of one filling to teeth would have doubled for the patient," Dr Abo Halima said.

"I am here, enduring the harsh summer heat, so that I can protect people from the high prices that I will inevitably have to charge if I rent an apartment, in addition to the fact that I have no other options at all."

Dr Abo Halima treats his instruments with care. He sterilises them regularly to protect them from dust and germs and hires a security guard. After all, the thin canvas walls offer little protection from thieves.

Despite his best efforts, the collapsed, resource-starved economy in Gaza means that dental care is a luxury for many patients.

One of them, 25-year-old Yousef Abo Halima, sums up the situation in a few simple words: "I can handle the harsh heat inside the tent, but I certainly cannot afford the high costs of fillings at clinics that operate inside apartments".

After Heba Rihan, 23, graduated from Al-Aqsa University with a major in general nursing, she struggled to find work in her field.

So she made an arduous daily journey from the south of the Gaza Strip to the west on foot, looking for work. She eventually found Dr Abo Halima's clinic in May and began working there.

Now, one of the most regular parts of her job is explaining to patients that the high cost of treatment is due to the scarcity of materials and other issues related to the war and Israel's siege on Gaza.

"One day [a patient] came in deep pain… When he asked how much the filling cost and was told it was 350 shekels ($116), he didn't have the money. He asked directly about the tooth extraction, which is only 50 shekels ($17)," she said.

"He decided to extract his original tooth because he could not bear the pain or the cost. That was the most painful moment I've ever had here."

articles.title: In 1964, a couple bought 535 acres in North Carolina and built a summer home there; decades later, they donated the entire property to Great Smoky Mountains National Park in its largest land gift since the park was created
articles.summary: US News: A high-altitude property first bought as a private family retreat in the mid-1960s now serves as an important centre for environmental research in Nor.
articles.body: A high-altitude property first bought as a private family retreat in the mid-1960s now serves as an important centre for environmental research in North America. The 535-acre property in Haywood County, North Carolina, historically known as "The Purchase", was officially transferred to the National Park Service around the turn of the millennium. Former owners Kathryn McNeil and Voit Gilmore donated the land, which became part of Great Smoky Mountains National Park. It was the largest single private land gift to the park since its establishment in 1934. Located along the Cataloochee Divide, the property sits on a high ridge next to the existing national park boundary. Its main landmark is Purchase Knob, a 5,086-foot peak offering wide views of the surrounding mountains.McNeil and Gilmore bought the property in 1964 and built a summer home on the mountain ridge. For almost four decades, the land was used as a quiet family retreat. In 2000, however, the owners decided to give up private ownership permanently to protect the area's high-elevation ecosystems for the future. According to records from the Great Smoky Mountains National Park website, the acquisition added important land to the federal park, which covers more than 520,000 acres across North Carolina and Tennessee. Park officials soon recognised the gift as an important addition to scientific research in the region.A permanent mountain research centreSoon after the land was transferred, the US Congress approved funding to create five specialised research centres across the national park system. In 2001, "The Purchase" was selected as the site of the Appalachian Highlands Science Learning Center. Instead of tearing down the original homes and buildings, the National Park Service adapted them for scientific research. Today, the former summer property includes offices, laboratories, a classroom that can hold 50 people and accommodation for up to eight visiting researchers at a time. The property also contains a preserved historic cabin that provides a glimpse into the area's earlier human history. The learning centre changed the main purpose of the ridge from private recreation to public scientific research. Its location gives researchers direct access to high-elevation environments that are especially sensitive to changes in climate, air pollution and biodiversity. About 5,000 people take part in programmes at the site each year, including scientists, teachers and school students. Research covers many areas of ecology, including changes in tree lines, lichen monitoring, insect studies and air quality.Preserving high-elevation habitatsThe environmental importance of the 535-acre property comes largely from its high and varied landscape. Mountain ridges above 5,000 feet in the Southern Appalachians support rare plants and animals, including species that survived from the last ice age. Before the land was donated, high-elevation areas outside the park faced continued pressure from developers looking to build luxury homes and resorts. By placing the property under federal protection, McNeil and Gilmore helped prevent the forest along the Cataloochee Divide from being broken into smaller sections. Scientists at the Appalachian Highlands Science Learning Center also study species that were not recorded in older park surveys. Through projects such as the All Taxa Biodiversity Inventory, researchers and students have identified thousands of organisms around Purchase Knob and nearby slopes, helping scientists understand the Smokies' complex ecosystems. The centre also gives young students opportunities to take part in scientific work. Field trips allow school groups from the region to collect information alongside professional biologists, giving them practical experience with field sampling and data collection.Legacy of the 2000 land giftThe size of the McNeil and Gilmore donation remains unusual in the modern history of the park. The creation of Great Smoky Mountains National Park in the 1920s and 1930s depended heavily on state funding, private donations and land purchases and condemnations. However, land additions of this size have become rare. More recent additions have generally involved smaller properties secured through conservation agreements or direct purchases by land trusts. In documents describing the history of the Appalachian Highlands Science Learning Center, park officials highlighted the lasting importance of the donation. The National Park Service says staff members and visiting researchers continue to use the facilities that were part of the family's original property. "Every day, the staff and program participants thank the family for their generous gift," the National Park Service says in its historical facility overview. What began as a private mountain property purchased in 1964 eventually became a permanent public resource for high-altitude research. The Appalachian Highlands Science Learning Center continues to operate throughout the year at Purchase Knob, supporting monitoring programmes, educational activities and field research developed over the past two decades.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Trump proposes stripping tax-exempt status from 18,000 schools over race-based benefits
articles.summary: US News: The Trump administration has proposed stripping private schools, colleges and other educational institutions of their tax-exempt status if they provid.
articles.body: The Trump administration has proposed stripping private schools, colleges and other educational institutions of their tax-exempt status if they provide admissions, scholarships or other benefits to students based on race.The proposed rule, announced by the Treasury Department on Thursday, could affect as many as 18,000 institutions and is part of President Donald Trump’s broader push to eliminate race-based diversity programmes in education, the Associated Press reported.Under the proposal, schools that provide benefits on the basis of race, colour or national or ethnic origin could lose their tax-exempt status. However, the rule would not cover religious institutions or race-neutral considerations such as family income, individual hardship, military family status or academic achievement.Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said institutions would not be able to avoid the proposed restrictions simply by changing the language used to describe race-based programmes.“Schools rebranding race-based preferences as equitable, inclusive, or diversity-enhancing does not change their discriminatory nature,” Bessent said.The proposal would apply to private primary and secondary schools, colleges, universities, professional schools and trade schools, including institutions that do not receive federal funding.Schools could face fundraising impactLosing tax-exempt status could have consequences beyond the taxes institutions themselves would have to pay. Donations to tax-exempt organisations are generally eligible for tax deductions, meaning schools could find it harder to attract contributions if donors lose that benefit.The administration has increasingly used federal policies to challenge diversity, equity and inclusion programmes at educational institutions. Trump has also targeted Harvard University in his broader dispute with colleges over what he has described as ideological and antisemitic problems on campuses.The proposed regulations are scheduled to apply to taxable years beginning on or after May 31, 2027, if they are finalised. The proposal will first go through a public comment process and could be modified before becoming final.Supreme Court ruling citedThe Treasury Department cited a 2023 Supreme Court ruling involving Students for Fair Admissions in support of the proposed regulations. The court ruled that colleges could not consider race in admissions decisions under the Equal Protection Clause of the 14th Amendment.The ruling directly concerned admissions, but its impact extended to other areas of higher education, including race-specific scholarships and financial aid programmes.There is also a historical precedent for the government revoking a college’s tax-exempt status. Bob Jones University lost its tax exemption in the 1970s after maintaining a policy banning interracial dating and marriage. The Supreme Court later upheld the IRS decision.Education leaders have criticised the latest proposal, warning it could create additional compliance requirements and uncertainty for colleges while affecting scholarship funding.The administration, however, has described the move as an effort to ensure that educational institutions follow federal civil rights requirements and restore merit-based policies.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
